An image is provided at `/app/media/image.png`.

You may open, crop or zoom it as needed.

## Question

## What to do

Write your answer to `/app/answer.md`.

**`/app/answer.md` is the only thing that is graded.** Nothing you print to the
terminal, and no other file, is read. If that file is missing or empty when you
stop, the task scores zero however good your analysis was.

You are working against a time limit and will be cut off without warning when it
is reached. So:

1. **Write a complete answer to `/app/answer.md` early** -- as soon as you have a
   defensible answer, before doing any deeper analysis.
2. Then investigate the media further and **overwrite the file** whenever your
   answer improves.

That way the file always holds your best answer so far, and being cut off costs
you refinement rather than the whole attempt. Answer in prose, and state each
point explicitly rather than implying it.

- **Relative to the people in the photo:** it is coming from behind and past the bride (the woman in the blue dress, on the left), blowing across the officiant in the middle and on towards the groom in the blue suit on the right.
- **What is *not* the case:** it is not blowing from the right towards the bride, it is not blowing straight into the camera, and it is not blowing from behind the camera into the scene. Every loose, freely hanging item in the frame is displaced towards the right, none towards the left.

It is genuinely light — a Beaufort force 1–2 "light air / light breeze" — not a gust. Full reasoning below.

## The evidence, item by item

**1. The bride's long skirt is swung to the right (the strongest single cue).**
I segmented the blue dress and measured the position of the skirt in every row of pixels from her hips (y ≈ 620) down to where the foreground boulder hides the hem (y ≈ 860):

- The centre-line of the skirt drifts steadily to the right as it descends — a lean of about **6.7° off vertical, roughly 28 px, which at the scale of this photo is about 10 cm of sideways offset at the hem**. Her head and hips are essentially plumb above one another, so this displacement is all in the skirt, not in her posture.
- More telling, the two sides do not move by the same amount. The **left-hand (upwind) edge leans 5.0°** while the **right-hand (downwind) edge leans 8.3°**, so the skirt is also slightly wider at the bottom on the right. That asymmetry is the classic signature of air pushing on a light skirt from one side: the windward face is pressed in against the leg while the leeward face balloons outwards. A skirt merely hanging over a forward-placed foot would swing without that flare asymmetry.

**2. The officiant's necktie hangs off-plumb to the right.**
A necktie is a free-hanging pendulum and therefore a good wind vane. Measuring the tie's centre-line down the blade, the tip sits about **4–5 px (≈5°) to the image-right of the knot**. Small — as it should be for a light breeze — but in the same direction as the skirt, and a tie has no "posture" excuse.

**3. The white garment draped over the green utility box at the far left of the frame** hangs down and away **to the right**, with its lower right corner lifted and flared out rather than hanging plumb against the box. This is on the opposite side of the frame from the bride, in a completely different air stream around a different obstacle, and it agrees.

**4. The apple tree filling the upper half of the frame is being ruffled.**
Across the canopy a very large fraction of the leaves are turned over, showing their pale, silvery undersides instead of the dark green upper surfaces — the standard visual signature of a breeze working through a broadleaf canopy, and the reason one can say at a glance that it is not a dead-calm day. The slender current-season shoots at the top of the crown are streaming up and to the right.

**5. Confirmation that the breeze really is only light.**
- There is **no motion blur anywhere in the foliage**. I measured the structure tensor (gradient anisotropy) over several leaf regions: coherence is only 0.03–0.07, i.e. gradients are essentially isotropic, so the leaves are frozen sharp with no directional streaking. Leaves silhouetted against the blue sky have crisp edges.
- The bride's **drop earring hangs almost exactly plumb** (about 3° off vertical) — but it is short, heavy for its area and tucked in against her jaw, so it is the item you would expect to move least.
- The deflections are all a few degrees, not tens of degrees. Nobody's hair is being thrown about, the officiant's sheet of paper is not flapping, and the heavy worsted trousers of both men hang straight.

## Things I ruled out before concluding

- **Camera roll.** If the camera had simply been held tilted, *everything* would lean the same way and the skirt measurement would be meaningless. It was not: the top line of the dry stone wall in the background, which is level in reality, is horizontal in the image to within about 1–2° over its whole visible length.
- **Perspective (converging verticals).** The camera is pitched slightly upwards, which makes true verticals converge towards the top of the frame. For an object 134 px left of the frame centre, at this focal length, that effect amounts to only about **3 px** over the height of the skirt — an order of magnitude smaller than the 28–36 px observed, **and it acts in the opposite direction** (it would tip her *left* at the bottom). So the real deflection is, if anything, slightly larger than measured.
- **Her stance.** A skirt draped over a forward-placed foot could account for part of the offset. That is why I did not rest the conclusion on the dress alone: the necktie, the draped white garment and the flare asymmetry of the skirt are independent of her stance and all point the same way.

## Limits of what the photo can tell us

- **No compass bearing is recoverable.** The file carries no EXIF, GPS or timestamp (it is a stripped PNG), and there is no landmark, signpost or shadow-plus-clock combination that would fix north. From the cast shadows on the lawn — the young apple trees throw their shadows to the left and slightly towards the camera — the sun is high and off to the right of the camera's line of sight, which means the breeze is blowing roughly from the shaded side of the scene towards the sunlit side. That is as far as it goes: converting it into "north-westerly", etc., would require knowing the time of day and the camera's heading, neither of which the image supplies.
- **The along-the-view-axis component is undetermined.** All the measurable deflection is sideways, so the wind is predominantly a cross-frame, left-to-right flow. A modest additional component blowing towards or away from the camera cannot be excluded from a single still image, but it is not what dominates.
